pixels.lens: Pixels and instrument. Every one of the 327 SPHEREx exposures (all six detectors, three visits) was measured with my own astropy/numpy/scipy code on the cached cutouts: aperture photometry, Gaussian centroid and width, flags, detector position, a crowded-field fit with the neighbouring stars modelled, blank-sky noise, a ghost-geometry test against bright stars within 0.6 degrees, the spectrum, and stamps that I looked at.

findings.what: The sweep's whole Aug-Sep 2025 row is light from a known, steady star, not from the candidate. That covers 'appears in 2025', D6 153, D5 187, D2 17 and D1 0.2 mJy. The star is 2MASS 18031245-2327467 (J 11.47, H 8.79, K 7.40) = AllWISE J180312.46-232746.7 (W1 6.66, W2 6.49 = 437 mJy, W3 5.20, W4 3.61) = Gaia DR3 4069173276061250560 (G 20.4). It lies 17.1 arcsec from the sweep's position. In every D6 exposure of visit 1, the light the sweep's aperture picks up has its centroid on that star, not on the candidate. The sweep's write-up never names this star; it names only the 11.6 and 12.4 arcsec W2 11.6 sources. The same star saturates D3 and D4 in 2025, which is why the sweep had 'none clean' there.
findings.evidence: measurements.json: D6 visit 1 centroids east -5.61 +/- 0.08, north +15.89 +/- 0.07 arcsec from the sweep's position (18 exposures). The 2MASS position is (-5.68, +16.11) and Gaia's is within 0.4 arcsec. The star's own aperture flux in D6 visit 1 is 444 mJy (control_stars.py), matching AllWISE W2 (437). calib.py: the neighbour is saturated within 1 px in D3 in 15 of 19 exposures and in D4 in 16 of 17 in visit 1. VizieR II/328 and II/246 rows in downloads/.

findings.what: The sweep's position is off by 3.1 arcsec, pulled toward that neighbour. The real source (A') sits 20.1 arcsec from the star. The sweep's aperture (radius 15.4 arcsec) mixes the two, so every number in its table is a blend, and its 9-fold ratio is wrong. Its Aug 2026 entries D4 306 (one exposure, centred on the neighbour), D3 150 and D2 11 are mostly or entirely the neighbour's light: measured at A', D2 is -1.0 (not detected) and D3 is 22 mJy.
findings.evidence: positions.py: A' median centroid in D6 visit 3 is RA 270.804063, Dec -23.468200 (20 exposures, 0.12 arcsec scatter each). measurements.json, D4 2026W35_2A_0544_1: the centroid falls on the neighbour (-5.40, +15.77). results_table.tsv: at A', Aug 2026 D2 is -1.0 mJy (18 exposures) and D3 is 21.9.

findings.what: Saturation and possible nonlinearity in spring 2026. At A', 10 of 18 D6 exposures and 16 of 18 D4 exposures are saturated, as are 13 of 19 D4 exposures in Aug 2026. All 18 D6 exposures in spring have OVERFLOW (half full well) pixels in the core. The 7 clean D6 values therefore rest on OVERFLOW pixels, so the spring brightness of about 2.8 Jy could be biased by nonlinearity. Fluxes fitted from the wings of the saturated exposures (2,500 to 7,300 mJy) are unreliable. I did not reproduce the sweep's whole-image lower limits of 2,576 and 3,272 mJy.
findings.evidence: calib.py and flagcount.py: D6 visit 2 has saturated pixels within 1 px of A' in 10/18 exposures and OVERFLOW in 18/18; D4 in 16/18 (visit 2) and 13/19 (visit 3). spectrum_table.tsv shows the saturated flags.

findings.what: The source probably brightened within the March 2026 visit, by about 1.8 times in 3.2 days at 4.42 to 4.45 micrometres. The paired D3 exposures show the same rise (1.3 times at 1.64 to 1.67 micrometres), which argues against a glitch in one detector. However, the later exposure falls 34 px from the detector edge, so this is not certain. Within the visit, wavelength and time also change together.
findings.evidence: spectrum_table.tsv: D6 2026W13_2A_0410_1 (MJD 61127.54, 4.454 um) 1900 mJy against 2026W14_1A_0357_1 (MJD 61130.73, 4.422 um, detector y 2006) 3490 mJy. D3 in the same two exposures: 92 against 123 mJy.

findings.what: The faint state is a real measurement: A' was absent in Aug-Sep 2025. Nothing at A' is saturated or OVERFLOW in any 2025 exposure. The crowded-field fit (neighbour modelled) gives values consistent with blank sky in every detector. So the rise at 4.4 to 5.0 micrometres is more than 200 times, not 9 times. D3 and D4 in 2025 are poorly constrained because the neighbour is saturated there.
findings.evidence: results_table.tsv, A' in visit 1: D6 -5.5 mJy (MAD 1.1, 18 exposures), D5 -7.6 (17), D2 -3.4, D1 -0.9. noise.py, 30 positions with no catalogued source, same exposures, median over the visit: D6 -1.7 +/- 1.8 mJy (largest of 30 is 14), D5 -2.2 +/- 2.2. A plain 2.5-px aperture is limited by crowding: blank-aperture scatter 28 mJy in D6 and 35 in D5 (measure.py). calib.py: within 1 px of A' in visit 1, 0 exposures saturated and 0 with OVERFLOW in every detector.

findings.what: It stays at one fixed place on the sky. The centroid agrees between visits, between detectors and within each visit, with no drift, and the image's astrometry matches 2MASS to 0.2 arcsec. A moving body or a blend whose members change brightness would drift.
findings.evidence: positions.py: D6 visit 3 east 1.46 +/- 0.12, north -2.70 +/- 0.12 arcsec (n=20). D6 visit 2 differs from visit 3 by 0.36/0.20 arcsec, D5 by 0.11/0.16. D2, D3, D4, D5 and D6 all agree within 0.4 arcsec. Drift in D6 visit 3 is -0.007 and +0.004 arcsec/day over 28 days. The neighbour's measured position is 0.07 and 0.22 arcsec from 2MASS.

findings.what: The instrument cannot fake it. In each visit A' fell at detector rows from about 16 to 2005, and the detector was turned 180 degrees between visits 2 and 3, yet the sky position stayed within 0.4 arcsec. That rules out persistence (which stays on fixed pixels) and two kinds of ghost: one at a fixed offset from its parent star, and one mirrored through the detector centre. In visit 1 the pointing was the same as in visit 3, with the brightest star at the same place relative to A' on the detector, and there was nothing at A'. The archive's ghost flag bits are not set at A' in any exposure.
findings.evidence: ghost.py. Detector angle 92.4 deg in visits 1 and 3, 271.7 in visit 2; detector x of A' about 250 (visit 2) and about 1005 (visit 3). The brightest star, 2MASS 18022364-2328350 (K 1.73, 11.3 arcmin away), is at offset (-111, +9) px in both visit 1 and visit 3. A fixed-offset ghost would land 22.6 arcmin from A' in visit 2; a mirrored ghost comes no closer than 14.9 arcmin. Same-geometry pairs: visit 3 gives 507 to 970 mJy, visit 1 gives -3.8 to -8.4 mJy, with A' 128 px apart on the detector. flagcount.py: no GHOST, GHOST_FPA or GHOST_EXT bits at A'.

findings.what: It is shaped like a star. In Aug 2026 its width and roundness match a known control star of similar brightness in the same exposures. In spring 2026 it is about 22% wider, which I attribute to the overflowed core; I did not test that.
findings.evidence: D6 visit 3: A' FWHM 8.11 arcsec (n=19), axis ratio 0.97; control star AllWISE J180315.97-232753.1 (W2 6.20, 43 arcsec east) 8.06 arcsec; the neighbour 8.5 arcsec; isolated field peaks 7.6 arcsec. D6 visit 2: A' 9.98 arcsec against the control star's 8.15.

findings.what: The brightness scale is steady between visits, and paired detectors agree. The control star stays constant to a few per cent in D6. The paired detectors (D2/D5, D3/D6, D1/D4) see A' at the same place at the same moments, and the rise appears in both members of a pair.
findings.evidence: control_stars.py: J180315.97-232753.1 in D6 reads 460, 487 and 466 mJy across the three visits. positions.py: in visit 2, D3 (1.64, -2.75) against D6 (1.82, -2.50), and D2 (1.58, -2.86) against D5 (1.61, -2.61) arcsec.

findings.what: The spectrum is a smooth red continuum, not an artefact. In Mar-Apr 2026 it rises from about 1 mJy at 1.0 micrometres to about 2,800 mJy at 5 micrometres; by Aug 2026 the 1.1 to 1.6 micrometre light is gone. No ice absorption is visible at 3.0, 4.27 or 4.67 micrometres (D4 is mostly saturated, so the 3.0 band is poorly sampled). Two single exposures show possible hydrogen emission lines: an excess at 4.04 to 4.06 micrometres (Br-alpha) in both 2026 visits, and one D3 exposure at 1.877 micrometres (Pa-alpha). Each is about 3.5 sigma and unconfirmed. If real, they would point to an eruption such as a nova; that is not established.
findings.evidence: spectrum.py and spectrum_table.tsv. Mar-Apr 2026: a pure blackbody gives T = 878 K, chi2/dof 3.2 (10% error floor; the within-visit rise worsens the fit). Aug 2026: pure blackbody 784 K (chi2/dof 0.90), or reddened 1040 K with A_K 1.85 (0.71); temperature and reddening are degenerate. 4.055 um, Aug 2026: 844 mJy against 663 and 689 in the neighbouring channels. 4.036 um, spring: 2439 against 1617 (3.966 um) in the same 7-minute sequence. 1.877 um: 554 against about 170 to 200 at 1.92 to 1.96 um. D2 in spring: 4 to 82 mJy over 1.11 to 1.63 um; in August, -1.0.

findings.what: At the sweep's own position, my independent aperture code reproduces the sweep's table. This shows the sweep measured correctly, but at the wrong place: what it measured is a blend.
findings.evidence: results_table.tsv, sweep position, 2.5-px aperture: D6 148.6, 2914.7 and 873.1 mJy (sweep: 153, 2915, 870); D5 188.1, 1901.4, 792.0 (187, 1903, 790); D2 18.6, 43.3, 11.1 (17, 42, 11); D4 single values 724.7 and 304.9 (729, 306); D3 649.9 in spring from 3 exposures (644). Not reproduced: D3 Aug 2026 150 (I find 0 clean exposures there).

findings.what: At the corrected position the sky is empty in the catalogues to their limits. Nothing in 2MASS, AllWISE or Gaia lies within 9.4 arcsec of A'. The bright neighbour is 20.1 arcsec away. CatWISE2020 could not be checked: the mirror returned header-only answers even for a control field.

pixels.could_not_check:
- CatWISE2020: the mirror gave no rows even for the control field.
- Optical ghosts from stars beyond 0.6 degrees, or from stars missing from 2MASS/AllWISE. SPHEREx's own ghost model is not available, and the archive sets no ghost flags.
- Nonlinearity of the OVERFLOW pixels that all the spring-2026 D5/D6 values rest on. The spring brightness (about 2.8 Jy at 4.4 to 5.0 micrometres) could be biased.
- The sweep's whole-image lower limits (2,576 and 3,272 mJy): not reproduced; I used cutouts only.
- Whether the 1.8-fold rise within the March 2026 visit is real: the only same-wavelength repeat lies 34 px from the detector edge.
- The Br-alpha and Pa-alpha excesses: each rests on single exposures at about 3.5 sigma.
- The 2025 faint state in D3 and D4: the saturated neighbour corrupts the fit there.
- My point-spread model is a Gaussian, corrected to the 2.5-px aperture with factors (1.14 to 1.22) measured on field stars.
- No search for reports, novae or variable-star listings was made at the corrected position; that belongs to another lens. Because the spectrum hints at hydrogen emission and an eruption-like light curve, that search should be redone at RA 270.80406, Dec -23.46820.

pixels.summary:
The brightening is real and instrument-independent, but the sweep reported the wrong place and the wrong history.

The sweep's position is 3.1 arcsec off. Its whole Aug-Sep 2025 detection ('appears in 2025', D6 153 mJy, D5 187, D2 17) is light from a known, steady star 17 arcsec away: 2MASS 18031245-2327467 / AllWISE J180312.46-232746.7, W2 6.49, about 437 mJy. In every 2025 exposure the light the sweep measured has its centroid on that star. The write-up never names it, and it is also why D3 and D4 had no clean 2025 reading.

At the true position, RA 270.80406, Dec -23.46820, the source (A') was absent in Aug-Sep 2025 (D6 -5.5 mJy against blank sky -1.7 +/- 1.8). It was about 2.8 Jy at 4.4 to 5.0 micrometres in Mar-Apr 2026 (partly saturated, probably still rising during that visit), and 0.8 Jy in Aug-Sep 2026, falling to about 0.55 Jy by 22 Sep. That is a rise of more than 200 times, not 9 times.

It is a point source fixed on the sky: 0.12 arcsec scatter per exposure, stable across visits and detectors, as wide as a control star. It stays put while the detector turns 180 degrees and while it moves across the whole detector. A year apart, with the same pointing and the same bright-star geometry, there was nothing in 2025 and 800 mJy in 2026. So it is not persistence, a ghost, a cosmic ray or a moving body. A control star stays within 5% across the visits.

The spectrum is a smooth, very red continuum (colour temperature about 800 to 1000 K), with possible hydrogen emission (Br-alpha at 4.05 micrometres in both 2026 visits, Pa-alpha in one exposure), which would be consistent with something like a dust-forming nova. That is a hint, not established.

No 2MASS, AllWISE or Gaia source lies within 9.4 arcsec of the true position; CatWISE could not be checked.

Verdict for this lens: survives, with caveats. The position and the whole brightness table must be corrected, the spring-2026 numbers rest on overflowed (half-full-well) pixels, and the report and nova search should be rerun at the corrected position.

On 'it is not even visible': in my stamps (stamps_D6_D4_D2.png) the object is plainly visible in 2026 in D6 and D4 (faint in D2 in spring) and absent in 2025. What looked like a source in 2025 is the neighbouring star.

archives.candidate: A: sweep position RA 270.80362, Dec -23.46745 (l 6.713, b -0.634). The 2026 SPHEREx centroid I measured, P, is RA 270.80409, Dec -23.46819 (18h03m12.98s -23d28m05.5s; l 6.7123, b -0.6352; ecliptic latitude -0.03 deg). P lies 3.1 arcsec from the sweep position at PA 150.
archives.lens: What was at this place before 2025: catalogues, pre-2025 images, upper limits, SIMBAD context.

findings.what: The sweep says A 'appears in 2025' at 153 mJy (D6) and 187 mJy (D5). Those numbers are real but they are not the candidate. They come from the edge of the light of a steady bright star, W, 17.0 arcsec from the sweep position. The sweep measures through a circle 15.4 arcsec in radius, so W's spillover lands inside it. The candidate was absent in Aug-Sep 2025, so the 'ninefold brightening' is wrong.
findings.evidence: I ran the project's own backend.photometry.measure on the cached Aug-Sep 2025 cutouts and reproduced C = 153 mJy (D6) and 187 mJy (D5). Control: the same measurement at 7 points that are also 17.0 arcsec from W, in other directions, gives D6 122-191 mJy (median 144) and D5 185-246 mJy. I also fitted two point sources at fixed positions (P and W) in each 2025 exposure. P comes out at -4.3 mJy in D6 (18 exposures, scatter 1.3) and -6.7 mJy in D5, while W comes out at 422 mJy. The Aug-Sep 2025 D6 median image (png/prior_images.png, bottom row) shows nothing at P. Files: tables/wing_test.json, tables/spherex_fixed_at_P.json.

findings.what: W is the brightest infrared source within 20 arcsec, and the sweep's catalogue check missed it. It is a steady, red, catalogued star 17 arcsec NNW of C and 20 arcsec from P. The sweep instead reported the nearest AllWISE source, at 11.6 arcsec with W2 11.6, and converted that to 0.4 mJy. The correct value is 3.7 mJy, ten times higher. The sweep also said GLIMPSE does not cover this longitude. That is wrong: GLIMPSE II covers it, with 55 catalogue rows and 79 archive rows within 30 arcsec.
findings.evidence: W's identifiers: AllWISE J180312.46-232746.7 (W1 6.662, W2 6.487 = 437 mJy, W3 5.200 = 263 mJy, W4 3.606 = 302 mJy, ph_qual AAAA), CatWISE J180312.48-232746.6 (W2 6.725), 2MASS 18031245-2327467 (J 11.47, H 8.79, Ks 7.40 = 728 mJy), GLIMPSE II [4.5] 6.32-6.37 in two epochs, MIPSGAL MG006.7158-00.6311 (24 um, 299 mJy), MSX G006.7156-00.6306, AKARI 1803124-232746. W is not in SIMBAD. NEOWISE measures W at W2 6.35-6.50 in all 21 visits from 2014 to 2024, and SPHEREx at 390-480 mJy in D5/D6 in all three epochs. Files: tables/gator_cand_*.tbl, consolidated_8as.txt.

findings.what: The sweep's position and its per-detector table are biased by W. The true centroid P is 3.1 arcsec SSE of C. All the sweep's per-detector numbers at C carry W's light in every epoch. This matters most for D2, D3 and D4 and for the Aug 2026 values: W itself is 300-625 mJy in D3.
findings.evidence: I fitted the position freely in each exposure. In Aug-Sep 2026 the D5/D6 position scatter is 0.2 arcsec, and the median is RA 270.80409, Dec -23.46819. To check SPHEREx astrometry, the same fit puts W 0.5 arcsec from its CatWISE position. With the project's aperture in Aug 2026, C reads 870 mJy and P reads 795 mJy, and the control points around W read 122-181 mJy. Files: tables/spherex_positions.json, tables/wing_test.json.

findings.what: No catalogue lists anything bright at P before 2025. The only sources within 3 arcsec are faint field stars. In K band (VVV, 2010-2019) the nearest is Ks 17.04 = 0.10 mJy at 1.5 arcsec, and it did not vary over 119 epochs. In the GLIMPSE II mid-infrared survey (2005-06) the nearest is [4.5] 14.35 = 0.33 mJy at 2.9 arcsec. Any of these could be a faint progenitor, but none is a pre-existing bright object.
findings.evidence: VIRAC2 (VizieR II/387): srcid 12989449006947 at 1.50 arcsec, Ks 17.04, H 18.01, 119 Ks epochs from MJD 55283 to 58363, etaKs 1.78. The brightest star within 3.2 arcsec is Ks 15.17 (0.57 mJy). VVV DR2: nearest is Ks 15.89 at 2.39 arcsec. GLIMPSE II: [3.6] 14.20 (0.59 mJy) at 2.61 arcsec and [4.5] 13.44 (0.76 mJy) at 4.13 arcsec. Nearest sources in the other surveys: 2MASS 9.44 arcsec, Gaia DR3 9.80, AllWISE 9.37, CatWISE 9.43, unWISE 7.41 (W2 12.23 = 2.2 mJy), Pan-STARRS 4.75 (y 20.2, one detection), SkyMapper 9.81. MIPSGAL 24 um has nothing within 19 arcsec except W. Hi-GAL has nothing within 60 arcsec. MSX, AKARI and IRAS list only W or nothing. Every query has a control row. File: tables/evidence_summary.csv.

findings.what: The pre-2025 images show the place empty in every band from 1.2 to 24 um. Only faint field stars sit at the edge of a 3 arcsec circle, and they are fainter than many stars nearby. P is not on a nebula, a cluster or the diffraction spike of a bright star. A smooth halo of W reaches toward P only at 24 um and 22 um.
findings.evidence: I looked at png/prior_images.png (2 arcmin field: 2MASS J/H/Ks 1998, IRAC 3.6-8.0, MIPS 24, WISE W1-W4 2010, and SPHEREx D6/D3 per epoch). I also looked at png/prior_zoom.png (40 arcsec field). Measuring at P in each image and calibrating against catalogued stars in the same image gives these 3-sigma upper limits: Ks <8.4 mJy (1998), [3.6] <3.4, [4.5] <2.1, [5.8] <1.9, [8.0] <2.2 and 24 um <10 mJy (2005-06), W3 <31 and W4 <170 mJy (2010, crude because of W's halo). File: tables/forced_phot.json.

findings.what: NEOWISE, 2014-03 to 2024-03: in 21 visits (280 frames) there is no detection within 3 arcsec of P at any date. One single-frame detection at 4.6 arcsec on 2019-08-31 (W2 9.90) does not repeat in the other frames of that visit. It is a passing transient (a moving object or a hit; P lies on the ecliptic), not a pre-existing source.
findings.evidence: Two neighbours, N1 and N2, 9.3 arcsec away with W2 11.5-11.7 (about 4 mJy), are detected in 246 and 257 of the 280 frames, and W is detected in every visit. So a source of 4 mJy or more at P would have been found. The 2019 row is 09087r139-008034, MJD 58726.936, sso_flg 0. I looked at the frame strip png/neowise_2019-08-31_visit.png: the object appears only in that frame, with a weaker excess one frame (1.6 h) later. Files: neowise_visits.txt, tables/gator_P_neowiser_p1bs_psd_r25.tbl.

findings.what: With the corrected baseline, the rise is much larger than the sweep says. At 4.4-5.0 um it is at least 200 times between Aug-Sep 2025 and Mar-Apr 2026 (7 months or less). It is at least 500 times relative to every NEOWISE visit from 2014 to 2024, and at least 1000 times relative to Spitzer in 2005-06. Near 2 um it is at least 300 times relative to VVV 2010-2019.
findings.evidence: Two-source fits at fixed positions, P: Mar-Apr 2026 D6 2926 mJy (scatter 1128; partly saturated) and D5 2281 mJy; Aug-Sep 2026 D6 670 and D5 541 mJy. Baselines: Aug-Sep 2025 under about 10 mJy; NEOWISE under about 4 mJy; IRAC [4.5] under 2.1 mJy. In D3: Mar 2026 about 180 mJy (scatter 151) and Aug 2026 about 20 mJy, against VVV Ks of 0.57 mJy or less within 3.2 arcsec. Zero points: 2MASS Ks 666.7 Jy; WISE W2 171.787 Jy; IRAC 280.9/179.7/115.0/64.13 Jy.

findings.what: Nothing known is catalogued at the place. SIMBAD and AAVSO VSX have nothing within 43 arcsec, ATLASGAL has nothing within 14.7 arcmin, and no VVV or UGPS high-amplitude variable is within 1 degree. The surroundings are a modest star-forming field: YSO candidates, Hi-GAL clumps 3.5 arcmin or more away, dark nebulae, HII regions about 8-10 arcmin away, and one OH/IR star at 9.8 arcmin. There are no masers, supernova remnants, planetary nebulae or clusters within 10 arcmin. This is context only, not proof of what the source is.

archives.summary:
Through this lens, A survives with caveats: nothing was at the place before 2026. The sweep's write-up of A is wrong, however, and needs correcting before anyone sees it.

**Nothing was there before.** At the true 2026 SPHEREx position P (RA 270.80409, Dec -23.46819, 3.1 arcsec from the sweep's position):
- In K band (VVV, 2010-2019) the only nearby stars are faint field stars, Ks 15.2 to 17 (0.1 to 0.6 mJy). The nearest, 1.5 arcsec away, did not vary over 119 epochs.
- At 4.5 um, Spitzer (2005-06) shows only sources of 0.3 to 0.8 mJy within 4 arcsec, and the image gives under 2.1 mJy at P.
- In 21 NEOWISE visits (2014-03 to 2024-03, 280 frames) nothing was detected within 3 arcsec, while 4 mJy neighbours 9 arcsec away were detected in about 90% of frames. So it was about 4 mJy or fainter at every visit.
- At 24 um, MIPSGAL gives under 10 mJy. Hi-GAL has no source within 60 arcsec.
- SIMBAD and AAVSO VSX have nothing within 43 arcsec. No catalogued VVV or UGPS high-amplitude variable lies within 1 degree.
- The pre-2025 images show P empty from 1.2 to 24 um.

**What is wrong in the sweep's write-up:**
- **The 2025 detection is not the candidate.** The 153 mJy (D6) and 187 mJy (D5) in Aug-Sep 2025 are light spilling from a steady bright star, W, 17 arcsec away (AllWISE J180312.46-232746.7, W2 6.49 = 437 mJy). The sweep measures through a 15.4 arcsec radius circle, wide enough to collect it. Running the project's own measurement code, I reproduced the 153 mJy. Seven control points the same distance from W in other directions give 122-191 mJy. A fit that models P and W separately gives -4 mJy at P in 2025.
- **The rise is far larger than ninefold.** The source was absent in Aug-Sep 2025 (about 10 mJy or less) and about 2.3 to 2.9 Jy at 4-5 um in Mar-Apr 2026. That is at least 200 times in 7 months or less, at least 500 times relative to every NEOWISE visit, and at least 1000 times relative to Spitzer. Near 2 um it is at least 300 times relative to VVV.
- **The catalogue check missed W.** W is the brightest infrared source within 20 arcsec, and it contaminates every per-detector number the sweep gives at its position.
- **Two smaller errors.** The nearest AllWISE source is 3.7 mJy, not 0.4 mJy. GLIMPSE II does cover this longitude.
- **The position is pulled toward W.** The sweep's position is off by 3 arcsec; P is the better one.

One NEOWISE detection near P, a single frame in 2019, does not repeat in the other frames of that visit. It is a passing event (the place is on the ecliptic), not an earlier source.

**Could not check:** UKIDSS GPS (empty answers), DECaPS (server error 502), unTimely (reachable but not downloaded), and VVV images. My own NEOWISE forced photometry failed its calibration check and is not used.

findings.what: The sweep's statement that the source appears in Aug-Sep 2025 at 153 mJy is wrong: that light comes from a steady, catalogued bright source 17.0 arcsec away. The sweep's catalogue summary left this source out; it named only the W2 11.6 sources at 11.6 and 12.4 arcsec. The source is AllWISE J180312.46-232746.7 (W2 6.49 mag, about 0.44 Jy), the same as CatWISE J180312.48-232746.6 and MIPSGAL MG006.7158-00.6311 (299 mJy at 24 micrometres). It sits 2.75 SPHEREx pixels away, on the edge of the sweep's 2.5-pixel aperture. At the target itself nothing is detected in 2025. The new source appeared between Sep 2025 and Mar 2026, when the field was close to the Sun from about November to January. The 2026 source is real and centred on the target. The 2025 colours the sweep quotes (D1 0.2, D2 17 mJy) are probably also the neighbour.
findings.evidence: My measurement on the 327 cached cutouts in backend/cache/sweep/cutouts/250d2b7784 (read-only), D6, medians per epoch. In Aug-Sep 2025 the aperture at the target gives 156.3 mJy, and the same aperture placed at the same distance from the neighbour in other directions also gives 156.3 mJy. The pixel value at the target minus local sky is 0.0 (D5) and 0.1 (D6) MJy/sr in 2025, against 412 and 559 in Mar-Apr 2026 and 185 and 182 in Aug-Sep 2026. In 2025 the centroid slides to the neighbour (median 0.5 arcsec from it). In 2026 it sits 2.8 arcsec (Mar-Apr) and 1.2 arcsec (Aug-Sep) from the target. The aperture on the neighbour gives 444 mJy in 2025, matching AllWISE W2, so the neighbour is steady. reports.summary:
I found no report or catalogue entry for a transient at this position. The checks that worked against their control novae were: TNS (60 arcsec and 1 degree), VSX (1 arcmin and 1 degree, no novae), ASAS-SN transients, CBAT TOCP, Mukai's confirmed and unconfirmed nova lists, three ZTF brokers, ATel titles and keywords for June 2025 to Nov 2026, arXiv searches, and six papers read, including the A&A young-star outburst paper (arXiv 2604.19551). Older catalogues show only faint, heavily reddened stars within 8 arcsec, so the place was never bright before. GLIMPSE does cover it, contrary to the sweep's note.

Caveats: SIMBAD failed its control (CDS was down and the CfA mirror lacks 2025 novae). ATel full text was blocked by a robot check, and ADS could not be searched. The ATel full-text and SIMBAD checks should be repeated by a person.

My own measurement on the cached cutouts corrects the sweep. Its Aug-Sep 2025 detection (153 mJy, 'appears in 2025') is the light of a steady catalogued source 17 arcsec away, which the sweep did not mention: AllWISE J180312.46-232746.7, W2 6.49 mag, about 0.44 Jy. The aperture flux at the target in 2025 equals the flux at mirror positions around that neighbour (156 mJy each), and the target pixel is at sky level. The real event is a new source centred on the target (within 1 to 3 arcsec) that rose from nothing to about 2.4 Jy at D6 in Mar-Apr 2026 and faded to about 0.86 Jy by Aug-Sep 2026. It began between Sep 2025 and Mar 2026. For this lens it survives, with caveats, as an unreported candidate. The sweep's description of the 2025 epoch and its 2025 colours must be corrected.

ordinary.candidate: A: sweep position RA 270.80362, Dec -23.46745 (l 6.713, b -0.634). My fit puts the source 3.0 arcsec away, at RA 270.80410, Dec -23.46814 (18h03m12.98s -23d28m05.3s), good to about 0.3 to 0.5 arcsec. Check on that: the bright neighbour comes out within 0.3 arcsec of its 2MASS and AllWISE positions with the same method.
ordinary.lens: Ordinary explanations, and what it probably is: Solar System body, a known variable or eruptive object, glare or a ghost from a bright star, which kind of object it is, and whether the rise shows in every detector

findings.what: The sweep's 2025 detection is not light from A. The 153 mJy (D6) and 187 mJy (D5) it measured in Aug-Sep 2025 come from the wing of a bright neighbour 17 arcsec from the sweep position (20 arcsec from A). The neighbour is 2MASS J18031245-2327467 (K 7.40) = AllWISE J180312.46-232746.7 (W2 6.49, about 436 mJy). A was absent in 2025. So the sweep's 'appears in 2025, brightens ninefold' is wrong. Corrected: absent in Aug-Sep 2025 and present by March 2026, at least 60 times brighter on a conservative limit and about 200 times or more on the forced fit.
findings.evidence: Model-free test: I re-ran the project's own aperture photometry at 9 control spots that sit at the same 17.1 arcsec from the neighbour. In 2025 they give a median of 142 mJy in D6 (range 123-180) against 153.3 at the sweep position, and 197 mJy in D5 (range 178-246) against 187.3. My forced two-source fit with fixed positions gives A in Aug-Sep 2025 of D6 -2.4 +- 2.8, D5 -3.0 +- 3.6, D4 -4.6, D3 -3.6, D2 -2.2, D1 -0.6 mJy. A single-Gaussian fit to the 2025 D5 and D6 exposures lands on the neighbour (dE -5.7, dN +15.8 arcsec, about 400 mJy in D6). Files: out/wingtest_summary.txt, out/forced_summary.txt, out/fit1_D56.csv, out/fit2_D56.csv, and the picture out/zoom_D5D6.png.

findings.what: The sweep's D2, D3 and D4 numbers are mostly the neighbour's light. D3 and D4 are 'none clean' in 2025 because the neighbour's saturated core and spilled charge fall inside the 15.4 arcsec measuring circle in all three visits, not because A was there. A's own D3 and D4 flux is 3 to 9 times below the sweep's table.
findings.evidence: Saturated pixels lie 8.8 to 14 arcsec from the sweep position in D3 and D4 in every visit (out/zoom_D3D4.png). The D3 Aug 2026 aperture value of 150 mJy equals the neighbour-wing control level of 146. Forced fit for A, March then August: D3 at 1.9-2.2 um 206 and 59 mJy (sweep: 644 and 150); D4 507 (one exposure) and 129-204 mJy (sweep: 729 and 306); D2 at 1.4-1.65 um 36 and 3 mJy. Median D6: 2419 and 685 mJy; D5: 1865 and 563 mJy.

findings.what: A small factual error in the sweep: it gives the nearest AllWISE sources' W2 11.6 mag as 0.4 mJy. It is 3.9 mJy.
findings.evidence: W2 zero point 171.79 Jy x 10^(-0.4 x 11.6) = 3.9 mJy. My own AllWISE query (VizieR II/328) gives the nearest sources at 9.47 and 9.54 arcsec from A, with W2 11.655 and 11.637.

findings.what: Not a Solar System body. A stays at the same sky position to about 0.3 arcsec between 2026 March 20 - April 1 and 2026 Aug 25 - Sep 22. JPL lists no known body near it at any visit.
findings.evidence: Two-component fits give a median position offset from the sweep position of (+1.64, -2.58) arcsec in D6 and (+1.77, -2.57) in D5 in March. In Aug-Sep it is (+1.42, -2.77) in D5 and D6, with scatter 0.13-0.15 arcsec (out/fit2_D56.csv). JPL sb_ident, geocentre, field +-3 arcmin, V<25: visit-1 midpoint (2025-09-01) none; visit-2 midpoint (2026-03-26) one body at 159 arcsec, V 24.1; visit-3 midpoint (2026-09-08) none; brightest exposure (2026-03-31 17:27) nearest (2014 EW81) at 54 arcsec, V 22.8. Control: the same request centred on Vesta's Horizons position returned 4 Vesta at 0.015 arcsec (downloads/jpl/).

findings.what: Not glare, a diffraction spike or a ghost of a bright star. A stays fixed on the sky while its place on the detector and the image orientation change completely. The same bright stars were present in 2025, when nothing was at A.
findings.evidence: The nearest stars with W2 < 4 or K < 5 within 0.5 deg are 9.8 arcmin away (W2 2.91, PA 308 deg), 11.3 arcmin (W2 -1.60 / K 1.73, PA 267 deg), 11.4 arcmin (W2 1.07) and 18.5 arcmin (W2 -1.89). A's detector position: x 243-584 in March, x 998-1449 in the 2025 and Aug 2026 visits, y 28-2005; the image orientation flips by 180 deg between seasons. Header 'L2 N_GHOST_FPA' = 0 in all 108 D5/D6 exposures (out/detpos.txt; downloads/gator_2mass_bright_30am.tbl, downloads/gator_allwise_bright_30am.tbl).

findings.what: No catalogued variable, long-period variable, OH/IR star, maser, young-star candidate, planetary nebula or X-ray source could be A. The only catalogued variable within 1 arcmin is 43 arcsec away and is a separate star.
findings.evidence: Within 60 arcsec: SIMBAD (CfA mirror) has only 2MASS J18031598-2327530, type LP?, at 43.0 arcsec (control: 330 objects within 15 arcmin). That is the same star as VSX 'Gaia DR3 4069172520146611584', type L, G 15.14-15.66, and Gaia DR3's LPV classification. SPICY, Robitaille+2008, the Engels & Bunzel maser database, Sevenster+1997 OH 1612 MHz, GCVS, Swift 2SXPS and 4XMM-DR13 have no rows; each has rows within 15 arcmin as a control. The Marton+2016 AllWISE young-star candidate list has only the bright neighbour (19.9 arcsec, class '?') and the 43 arcsec star. Acker PNe, Chandra CSC2, ROSAT 2RXS and Lucas+2017 have no rows even within 15 arcmin, so they give no control (out/vizloop.txt, out/vizloop2.txt, downloads/simbad_60as.csv).

findings.what: Before the outburst there was nothing brighter than about 0.3-1 mJy at 4.5 um or K about 15 at A's position. A Mira, OH/IR star or other long-period variable bright enough to reach 2.4 Jy would sit at 0.4 Jy or more even at minimum, and every infrared catalogue would list it. They do not, so those are excluded. The 4.5 um amplitude is at least about 8.5 mag.
findings.evidence: 2MASS (my IRSA query): nothing within 9.59 arcsec; a K 14.64 source is listed at 9.7 arcsec. VVV DR2 (II/348): nothing within 2.58 arcsec; nearest Ks 15.79 at 2.6, Ks 15.21 at 3.1, Ks 15.62 at 3.6 arcsec. GLIMPSE (II/293, all releases; the sweep asked only the first): nearest are [3.6] 14.20 at 2.76 arcsec and [3.6] 14.55 / [4.5] 14.35 (0.33 mJy) at 2.96 arcsec. AllWISE: nothing within 9.47 arcsec. Gaia DR3: nothing within 9.69 arcsec.

findings.what: NEOWISE 2014-2024 saw nothing at A in 20 of 21 visits, while 4 mJy stars 9 arcsec away were detected every time. One visit has two isolated single-frame red detections nearby, which are probably merged or artefact detections, not an earlier outburst.
findings.evidence: My Gator query (neowiser_p1bs_psd, 25 arcsec): 21 visits from 2014-03 to 2024-03. The neighbour (W2 6.4) is detected 11-22 times per visit (control), and the W2 11.5-11.9 stars at 9.3 arcsec 18-40 times per visit. Within 6 arcsec of A, only in the 2019-08-31 to 09-07 visit: MJD 58726.936, W2 9.903 +- 0.048 (19 mJy), W1-W2 2.4, at 4.7 arcsec, in a frame where the 9 arcsec stars were not separately detected. A second detection 6.7 arcsec away comes 1.6 h later in a qual_frame 0 frame. The other 10 frames of that visit show nothing. The sweep's cached 2015-09-15 row at 7.1 arcsec carries the W2 diffraction-spike flag 'd'.

findings.what: Not microlensing.
findings.evidence: Even with the conservative 2025 limit of 40 mJy, the magnification would have to be at least 60 in late March and at least 17 at Aug 28 (685 mJy), at least 155 days later. Keeping the impact parameter u <= 0.06 that long needs a timescale tE >= about 2,600 days, far longer than bulge events. The colour also changed: the colour temperature fell from 878 to 794 K, and the 1.1-1.4 um excess disappeared.

findings.what: The rise is real in every detector at once and is not a calibration error. A is near zero in all six detectors in 2025, detected in D2 to D6 in 2026, and fades smoothly with wavelength. The neighbour measured in the same exposures stays constant to about 10%.
findings.evidence: Neighbour, D6: 410, 382, 377 mJy; D5: 540, 491, 504 mJy in the three visits. A's fading from March to August: 1.4-1.65 um 2.8 mag; 1.65-1.9 um 1.3; 1.9-2.2 um 1.4; 2.2-2.5 um 1.6; 3.8-4.1 um 1.0; 4.1-4.42 um 1.35; 4.42-4.7 um 1.1; 4.7-5.0 um 1.5. D5 and D6 agree where they overlap in August (4.417 um: 670; 4.426-4.436 um: 620-680 mJy).

findings.what: The spectrum shows hydrogen in emission: a Br-alpha (4.05 um) excess in two visits, each in exposures taken minutes apart, with the neighbour flat in the same exposures. Pa-alpha (1.875 um) is suggestive. This means ionised gas, which suits a nova or a young-star outburst and argues against a pure dust or merger spectrum.
findings.evidence: Aug 30, 2026, three D5 exposures within 4 min: 547.5, 708.1 (band 4.037-4.073 um) and 572.5 mJy, a 26% excess at 4.4 sigma; the neighbour reads 544.6, 525.6, 504.2. Mar 25: 3.966 um then 4.036 um (band 4.018-4.054) four minutes apart, 1408 then 2055 mJy (+46%), while the neighbour went 629 to 560. Pa-alpha: Aug 27, 1.812 then 1.854 um two minutes apart, 24 then 52 mJy. One +3.4 sigma excursion at 3.864 um matches no line, so false positives are possible (out/lines.txt).

findings.what: The light is warm dust. Single blackbody fits per visit (using A's own fluxes) give the temperatures, luminosities and sizes below. 'What it probably is', ranked: 1) a heavily obscured classical nova that formed dust; 2) an embedded young-star outburst of EX Lupi type (disfavoured); 3) a stellar merger, i.e. a luminous red nova (possible, less likely). FU Orionis type, X-ray binary, symbiotic, R CrB and dust-enshrouded giant are excluded or disfavoured. No published example matches cleanly. In V5668 Sgr the dust cooled from 1090 to 720 K in 31 days; A's colour temperature fell only about 100-200 K in 5 months. That tension is unresolved.
findings.evidence: Fits, March 25-29 then August (out/sedfit.txt, picture out/sed_A_by_visit.png). Temperature: 878/794 K with no extinction; 925/828 K at A_K 0.27 (3 kpc); 1220/1018 K at A_K 1.53 (8 kpc); 1330/1080 K at A_K 1.86 (10.5 kpc or more). Extinction left free: A_K 0.0 +- 0.3 in March and 0.9 +- 0.5 in August. Luminosity: about 500 / 6,800 / 19,000 Lsun in March and 180 / 2,200 / 5,900 Lsun in August at 3 / 8 / 12 kpc; blackbody radius 4 / 9 / 12 au. Extinction inputs: Nishiyama+2009 law (arXiv:0902.3095, A_J:A_H:A_Ks:A_3.6:A_4.5 = 3.02:1.73:1:0.50:0.39, A_Ks/E(J-Ks) = 0.528). A_K at each distance from Schultheis+2014 (J/A+A/566/A120) at l 6.7, b -0.6: E(J-K) 0.513 at 3.0-3.5 kpc, 2.898 at 8.0-8.5, 3.517 at 10.0-10.5. Published comparisons: in nova V5668 Sgr, dust condensed by day 82 at 1090 K and was at 720 K by day 113 (Gehrz+2018, arXiv:1804.00575). Over half of the near-infrared-found Gattini-IR novae have A_V of 5 mag or more (De+2021, arXiv:2101.04045). FU Ori has faded only about 14 mmag per year, and FU Orionis stars show CO absorption, which excludes FU Orionis type given A's 1.4 mag fade in 5 months. EX Lupi rose to peak in 3-4 weeks, stayed high 6 months and reached about 5 mag in V; EX Lupi-type stars show CO emission (Audard+2014). But A's 4.5 um amplitude of at least 8.5 mag, the absence of any young-star progenitor or star-formation tracer, and a luminosity of at least 500 Lsun even at 3 kpc argue against that. The merger V1309 Sco had about 800 K dust after outburst but a cool M-type remnant (Nicholls+2013), which is less expected with hydrogen emission. Symbiotic star and R CrB are excluded: no giant brighter than K 15 within 2.5 arcsec. X-ray binary is disfavoured: the shape is a ~900 K blackbody, not a disc or jet, and no X-ray catalogue source lies within 60 arcsec.

findings.what: Timing: an eruption between visits could easily have gone unseen from the ground. The Sun passed 0.7 deg from A on 2025-12-22, and A was within 45 deg of the Sun from about Nov 8, 2025 to Feb 4, 2026. A was possibly still brightening at the end of March. It is near the Sun again now (about 38 deg in mid-November 2026), so ground follow-up is awkward until about Feb 2027.
findings.evidence: Solar separation computed with astropy get_sun every 7 days. At 4.42-4.52 um, D6 read 1,670-1,900 mJy on Mar 28 and 3,140 mJy on Mar 31, while the neighbour stayed at 380-395 mJy in the same exposures. Fading: 0.27 mag per month in D6 and 0.25 in D5 from March to August; 0.52 mag in 27 days at 4.436 um between Aug 25 and Sep 22 (680 to 421 mJy).

ordinary.summary:
Through this lens, A is not explained by any ordinary known thing, so it survives as a candidate. But the sweep described it wrongly.

What it got wrong: its 2025 "detection" (153 mJy in D6, 187 in D5) is the wing of a bright catalogued neighbour 17 arcsec from the sweep's position (20 arcsec from the source itself): 2MASS J18031245-2327467 = AllWISE J180312.46-232746.7, K 7.40, W2 6.49. Nine control spots at the same distance from that neighbour give the same flux (D6 median 142 mJy), and my forced two-source fit gives A at about 0 in every detector in 2025. The neighbour also accounts for most of the sweep's D3 and D4 values, including the 2025 "none clean". The source's true position is RA 270.80410, Dec -23.46814, 3 arcsec from the sweep's. The sweep also converted W2 11.6 to 0.4 mJy; it is 3.9 mJy.

Corrected picture:
- Absent in Aug-Sep 2025.
- About 2.4 Jy at 4.7 um in late March 2026, possibly still rising.
- 0.69 Jy in late August and 0.42-0.52 Jy on Sep 22.
- Before 2025 it was fainter than about 0.3-4 mJy in 2MASS, VVV, GLIMPSE, AllWISE and 20 of 21 NEOWISE visits. The amplitude at 4.5 um is at least about 8.5 mag.

Ordinary explanations ruled out, each with my own evidence:
- Solar System body: the position is fixed to 0.3 arcsec between visits five months apart, and JPL lists no known body within 54 arcsec (its control recovered Vesta).
- Ghost or glare: A stays fixed on the sky while its detector position and the image orientation change completely, and the nearest bright star is 9.8 arcmin away.
- Calibration error: the rise appears in D2 to D6 together, while the neighbour stays constant in the same exposures.
- Known variable: the only one within 1 arcmin is a separate long-period variable 43 arcsec away. No maser, OH/IR, young-star, planetary nebula or X-ray source lies within 60 arcsec.
- Mira or OH/IR star: it would be in every catalogue.
- Microlensing: it would need a timescale of 2,600 days or more, and the colour changed.

What it probably is:
- The light is warm dust, about 880-1,300 K in March cooling to about 800-1,100 K in August depending on extinction. That is a luminosity of about 500 / 6,800 / 19,000 Lsun at 3 / 8 / 12 kpc, fading 0.25-0.58 mag per month.
- Hydrogen Br-alpha is in emission (4.4 sigma in exposures minutes apart, neighbour flat).
- My ranked reading: a heavily obscured classical nova that formed dust, with the eruption possibly hidden by solar conjunction (the Sun passed 0.7 deg from it on 2025-12-22). Next, an embedded young-star outburst of EX Lupi type, which is disfavoured. Then a stellar merger (luminous red nova), possible but less likely. FU Orionis type is excluded by the fast fade. X-ray binary, symbiotic and R CrB are disfavoured or excluded.
- The decisive observation is a near-infrared spectrum at R of about 1000 or more. Broad hydrogen, He I and O I lines would mean a nova; CO bandheads with narrow Br-gamma, a young star; M-type CO and H2O absorption, a merger.
- A is about 38 deg from the Sun now, so the practical window opens around Feb 2027.

I did not check whether it has already been reported (OGLE, VVVX, Gaia alerts, PRIME, TNS); that belongs to another lens.

This step does not address the relayed user message about something in the app changing and not being visible.
